newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen guerrilla vows attacks on Russia cities.
newsitem.headline: Chechen guerrilla vows attacks on Russia cities.

text.p: Salman Raduyev, the hardline rebel fighter who led a bloody hostage raid a year ago, said on Wednesday he did not recognise Chechen elections held on Monday and was planning new terror attacks on Russia.
"At least three Russian cities must be burned to cinders," Raduyev told Reuters. "We are working on a major operation codenamed 'Ash'."
He was speaking in his village in eastern Chechnya two days after Chechnya held its presidential election in which moderate military commander Aslan Maskhadov scored a sweeping victory.

Raduyev, who believes that Chechya's first separatist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev reported killed in a Russian rocket attack last year is still alive, said he would not obey the new Chechen president and would carry out his own war against Russia.

"I obey no authority except all-highest Allah and Dzhokhar Dudayev...the freedom struggle will go on," said the guerrilla, who has worn dark glasses since last summer, when he reappeared with a face transformed by plastic surgery after being shot in the head in an attack by unidentified gunmen.
Raduyev has a record of successful operations carried out by his "Lone Wolf" group in the war which started in December 1994 when Russia sent troops to quell Chechnya's independence bid.

He won prominence after the "Lone Wolf" raided neighbouring ethnic republic of Dagestan in January 1996, held hundreds of hostages there and later escaped safely though the lines of Russian commandos who believed they had encircled the rebels.
"The Chechen conflict has born a new form of warfare -- military terrorism," said Raduyev, dressed in a grey military uniform.
"This means the destruction of Russian cities. We are preparing for this. As long as Moscow does not recognise unequivocally the political independence of our state Russia will remain our enemy."
At least two of Russia's towns and one village have suffered from rebel attacks during the unpopular Chechen war.

Field commander Shamil Basayev, one of the leading candidates in Monday's election, raided the southern town of Budennovsk in 1995 seizing hundreds of hostages and forcing Moscow to start peace talks.
Raduyev seized hostages in the Dagestani town of Kizlyar and later entrenched in the village of Pervomaiskoye, which Russian artillery practically flattened trying to force out the rebels.

Raduyev's ventures won him popularity in Chechnya but the unruly guerrilla, who refused to obey anyone's commands, has become a headache for other rebel leaders after they had struck a peace deal with Russia and started preparing for polls.
Under the deal signed on August 31 Russia withdrew its forces from Chechnya and the rebels agreed to postpone the decision on the region's future political status by five years.
Last December Raduyev's fighters seized 22 Russian police officers who tried to prevent them from entering Dagestan.

Maskhadov and acting Chechen President Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev forced him to set the prisoners free. Maskhadov later vowed that he will put an end to uncontrolled activities by independent-minded field commanders.
